cards.title: Meta's four-step ad serving pipeline
cards.summary: Retrieval, light ranking, heavy ranking and auction are the four stages Meta runs in roughly 200ms to pick which ad serves to a user.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a new ad gets no delivery, or setting expectations for how long creative needs to prove itself before you judge it.
steps: Map your ad's journey to the four stages. Retrieval: Meta scans tens of millions of ads to check basic relevance and to read your creative for targeting signals. Light ranking: cuts millions down to roughly thousands. Heavy ranking: cuts to a few hundred real competitors using the Total Value equation. Auction: remaining advertisers compete on bid, highest total value wins the impression.

Use heavy ranking's narrowing to reset competitiveness framing: only a handful of advertisers (Meta says roughly 10 million total advertisers platform-wide, far fewer in any ecommerce niche) are your actual rivals for a given impression, not the whole platform.

Use retrieval mechanics to explain flat delivery on a narrow manual ad set: if the creative's own signals (casting, script, thumbnail, copy, landing page) point to a small audience, retrieval can limit supply regardless of budget.
Accept that a losing ad is served lower-quality impressions rather than no impressions at all, so weak creative shows up as poor placement quality and rising cost before it shows as zero delivery.
caveats: The 200ms window, the rough ad-count stages (millions > thousands > hundreds) and the 10-million-advertiser figure are the presenter's simplified illustration of Meta's documented process, not a published benchmark.

cards.title: The Total Value equation behind every winning impression
cards.summary: Meta's Total Value equals (advertiser bid x estimated action rate) plus user value, so improving CTR and funnel conversion raises your effective bid without raising your bid.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise bids or fix creative and post-click conversion when an ad set cannot spend or CPA is too high.
steps: Write the formula where you plan media: Total Value = (Advertiser Bid x Estimated Action Rate) + User Value/Experience.

Expand Estimated Action Rate for a conversion-optimized campaign: Estimated CTR x Estimated Click-to-Conversion Rate. For ecommerce this means click-through to purchase; for lead-gen it means click-to-call or click-to-application, but the structure is the same.

Treat Estimated CTR as a bundle of soft engagement signals, not just link CTR: include CPC, CPM, hook rate, hold rate and cost per 3-second video view. Improving these lifts the first half of the equation.
Treat Estimated Click-to-Conversion Rate as your funnel's monetization. Improving PDP conversion, offer clarity or checkout completion lifts the second half.
Compare growth levers honestly: raising bid is one input; raising estimated action rate is two inputs (CTR and conversion rate) and compounds the same equation.
Keep user value in mind as Meta's own guardrail: it suppresses aggressive, low-quality advertiser experiences, so misleading creative that wins clicks but harms experience eventually costs delivery.
caveats: The equation came from Meta documentation that Meta later withdrew from its own site; treat the exact form as the presenter's best reconstruction. Estimated action rate is Meta's model, not a number you can read directly.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Creative is the targeting: broad targeting after Andromeda
cards.summary: Meta now reads creative elements to determine audience, making heavy manual interest and lookalike audience structures largely redundant for most ecommerce accounts.
cards.use_when: Structuring a new Meta ad account or rebuilding a legacy one built on stacks of interest and lookalike audiences.
steps: Assume retrieval parses your creative for targeting signals: casting (e.g. a 55-year-old woman in the ad skews delivery toward older women), format, hook, copy, script, thumbnail and even the landing page.

Default to broad targeting within Advantage+ campaigns rather than layering interests and lookalikes. The presenter reports rarely using interests and, when he does, capping their budget, and running retargeting audiences completely broad with at most one purchaser exclusion.

Allow Meta a reasonable degree of control, but audit automated suggestions: the presenter warns that many Facebook recommendations that promise a lower cost per result have damaged accounts, so verify against your own data before applying.
Reallocate time saved on audience building into creative volume and variety, since retrieval's inputs are creative elements you control.
caveats: This is the presenter's own operating pattern and observation about high-spend advertisers he speaks to, not a controlled test; manual audiences can still serve as a small experimentation sandbox. Advantage+ and targeting interfaces change, so verify current controls before rebuilding.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Andromeda changed retrieval, not the value of variations
cards.summary: The Andromeda update to retrieval made Meta lean harder on creative for targeting, but variations within a concept remain the highest-leverage way to get more at-bats.
cards.use_when: Planning a creative testing roadmap and deciding how many net-new concepts versus variations to launch each week.
steps: Understand the driver: a flood of AI-generated creative pushed Meta to update how retrieval sorts ads (Andromeda), shifting targeting weight from ad set settings toward creative elements.
Structure an ad set as one net-new concept containing three to four ad variations, so the concept gets multiple hooks and the algorithm gets more chances to find a winning combination.

When a concept looks like a loser, check whether variations inside it never got a fair test. The presenter's example: an original concept loses while a variation of that same concept wins, which you would never learn if you only tested net-new concepts.
Manage expectations on variation upside: per the presenter, a variation of your current top ad typically performs decently but usually will not beat the top ad.
Ignore the popular post-Andromeda narrative that variations are dead and only net-new concepts matter; the presenter calls that oversimplified and still runs variations.
caveats: Andromeda's internal behavior is not publicly documented in detail; the presenter explicitly attributes this reading to inference about the AI-creative flood. The variation-versus-top-ad observation is the presenter's experience, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Choosing auto-bidding versus cost caps and bid caps
cards.summary: Lowest-cost auto bidding and manual cost or bid caps both run profitable accounts at very high spend, so pick the method that solves your actual constraint.
cards.use_when: Deciding bidding strategy for a new campaign or when a stalled ad set needs a different bidding lever.
steps: Know the three options: lowest cost (auto bidding, Meta bids for you to get conversions as cheaply as possible), cost caps (a maximum you will pay to acquire a customer), and bid caps (a maximum bid to acquire a customer). Meta also offers target-ROAS and maximum-value style options that change over time.

Do not treat cost caps or bid caps as a required maturity step. The presenter reports running accounts spending multiple five figures per day, and others at six figures per day, entirely on lowest cost and remaining profitable, while other advertisers run only bid caps.

Choose based on the business constraint, not on what is trendy. If the constraint is protection against CPA spikes on a scaling campaign, a cost cap addresses that; if the constraint is simply more volume at efficiency, lowest cost is often enough.

Think like an entrepreneur about the growth problem. Manual bidding moves the needle marginally; the presenter says media buying is not dead but it cannot be the whole answer to going from 1K to 10K per day.
caveats: The presenter states no universal best bidding method; the high-spend examples are his experience, not guarantees. Manual bidding options and their availability change inside Meta Ads Manager, so verify the current interface before relying on a specific cap type.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Stop optimizing to leave the learning phase
cards.summary: Ads keep learning for their whole life, so rule on 7-day and longer windows of spend instead of reacting to daily swings, especially at low budgets.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to kill an ad or ad set after volatile daily ROAS, particularly in accounts spending under about $1,000 per day.
steps: Accept that Meta's stated learning phase is a rough model. The presenter's position: your ads never stop learning, and everything eventually declines regardless of whether it technically exited learning.

Expect volatility as normal at low spend. Up to roughly $1,000 per day, sine-wave results day to day are typical; the presenter views inconsistent daily results even well above that spend level as part of the platform.
Zoom out before making changes: evaluate on a 7-day window and on the largest spend window you have data for, rather than acting on one good or bad day.
If results are genuinely poor over a proper window, consider the simpler fix the presenter favors: make better ads rather than chasing learning-phase mechanics.
caveats: The ~$1,000/day figure is the presenter's informal rule of thumb for when daily volatility should be expected, not a calculated threshold from the source. Learning-phase requirements in Meta's own documentation may differ; verify in the current Ads Manager.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Set bidding strategy to your business constraint, not a trend
cards.summary: Pick auto bidding or manual caps based on the specific constraint in the store's ad account rather than adopting whatever manual bidding method is currently popular.
cards.use_when: Reviewing bidding strategy across a portfolio of campaigns or when a scaling campaign needs a guardrail on CPA.
steps: Name the constraint before choosing a method: is the problem volume (needs more spend), CPA protection (needs a ceiling), or efficiency at scale?

Match method to constraint: lowest cost auto bidding for volume at efficiency, cost caps for a customer-acquisition ceiling, bid caps for a bid ceiling, and target-ROAS or maximum-value options where the business goal is return-based.

Refuse to copy tactics from other accounts without context. The presenter notes accounts spending multiple five figures per day profitably on lowest cost and accounts run entirely on bid caps; both work in the right situation.
Revisit bidding strategy when the constraint changes, e.g. when moving a proven campaign from testing budgets to a growth budget where CPA protection matters more than raw spend.
caveats: No method is presented as universally superior; the presenter explicitly rejects the idea that manual bidding is the sophisticated upgrade. Method availability and naming inside Meta change frequently, so verify the current interface.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Push broad control to its limit, but audit Meta's suggestions
cards.summary: Give Meta enough control to let the algorithm work, but systematically reject automated recommendations that are not backed by your own account data.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Meta's automated recommendations and Advantage+ suggestions before applying them to a live store account.
steps: Set a default posture: run broad with limited manual constraints, because the algorithm performs well when it has room to optimize.

Before applying any Meta suggestion (e.g. a change it claims will lower cost per result by a specific percentage), require evidence from your own account rather than accepting the platform's projection.
Treat the recommendation surface as a sales channel, not advice: the presenter's framing is that Meta is a for-profit company and you are its paying customer, so suggestions can be self-serving.
Track what happens after applying suggestions so you build your own record of which recommendation types help or hurt in your account, instead of relying on the platform's stated uplift.
caveats: This is the presenter's strong opinion, supported by his own account history, not a controlled study. Some automated suggestions do help; the instruction is to test, not to refuse everything. Recommendation UI and claims change, so verify in the current interface.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Attribute conversions outside Facebook and read conversion data sceptically
cards.summary: Post-click conversion reporting inside Facebook is unreliable after iOS tracking changes, so judge performance with third-party attribution while still sending Meta good signal.
cards.use_when: Deciding which numbers to trust when reporting store performance or judging whether a Meta campaign is actually profitable.
steps: Do not steer the account on Facebook's own post-click CPA. The presenter does not look at Facebook CPA at all and relies on third-party attribution tools such as Triple Whale or Hyros, or a custom-built alternative.
Keep sending high-quality data back to Meta anyway, via the Conversions API (server-side plus browser) so Meta can learn about your customers and improve long-term delivery efficiency.

Check the purchase event in Events Manager for Event Match Quality (EMQ) on a 1-10 scale, but treat it as directional rather than causal. The presenter calls the concept overrated and reports running an account with EMQ in the 9.8-9.9 range without seeing a direct profit correlation.

Apply the same scepticism to other Meta quality scores: the presenter shows a profitable ad account displaying a zero opportunity score, which he uses as evidence that platform scores do not map directly to profitability.
Reconcile the two ideas: send good data because it is low-cost and directionally sensible, but take every conversion figure from Meta with a grain of salt and attribute with an outside source.
caveats: The presenter explicitly says the EMQ-to-profit relationship is not a direct correlation and gives his own counterexample; do not treat a high EMQ as a performance guarantee. Third-party attribution tools and Events Manager fields change, so verify current setup guidance.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Send first-party signal via the Conversions API even when attribution is uncertain
cards.summary: Server-side event sending improves the data Meta learns from, so implement it as hygiene while keeping your trust in Facebook-reported conversions low.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing a store's Meta tracking foundation before scaling spend.
steps: Confirm a Conversions API setup exists alongside the browser pixel, so purchase and other events reach Meta server-side rather than only from the browser.
Locate the purchase event in Events Manager and note the Event Match Quality score to confirm data is flowing, using it as a plumbing check rather than a profit forecast.
Judge results with an independent attribution source, since iOS opt-out reduces the completeness of Facebook's own conversion reporting.

Recognize the presenting trade-off: better data may improve Meta's ability to find customers long term, but the presenter has not observed a direct correlation between very high EMQ and profitability.
caveats: The presenter admits he cannot show a direct correlation between server-side setup quality and results and calls the concept overrated. The iOS 14.5 timeframe and opt-out mechanics belong to broader measurement topics; here the relevant action is simply having a server-side path in place.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Model every ad against the three takeaways of the auction
cards.summary: Creative acts as targeting, strong soft metrics supply half the total value equation, and respecting user experience protects long-term delivery.
cards.use_when: Briefing creative or auditing an account structure before committing budget to a store's next campaign push.
steps: Audit targeting structure first: minimize ad set fiddling with interests, custom audiences and lookalikes, and let creative signals define the audience. Broad is the default; audience layering is a small sandbox, not the strategy.

Audit creative against the first half of the value equation: does the ad stop the scroll and generate high CTR and other soft engagement metrics (hook rate, hold rate, cost per 3-second video view)? The presenter calls this roughly half the battle.
Audit user experience: ads that win cheap clicks by misleading users work against Meta's user-value term and can reduce long-term delivery quality.
Use the three takeaways as a pre-launch checklist before scaling, rather than as post-mortem analysis after poor performance.
caveats: These are the presenter's distilled takeaways, framed as opinion and experience, not measured principles. Soft metrics are one input among several in the equation.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Treat ad rejections and ban waves as timing and account scale, not pure fault
cards.summary: Meta's enforcement tightens or loosens around business cycles, so identical creative can be approved for one advertiser and rejected for another.
cards.use_when: Planning risk mitigation for a store's ad account, page or business manager after a rejection or ban.
steps: Stop treating a single rejection as proof the creative violates policy. The presenter's stated explanation is that enforcement and ban waves correlate with Meta's earnings reports: after weak reports, guidelines tighten and bans spike, then relax again weeks later.

Prepare operationally for the cycle rather than trying to find the perfect compliant creative: because identical ads can be approved or rejected depending on timing, redundancy across ad accounts, pages and business managers matters.

Do not expect the enforcement pattern itself to be knowable; the presenter's core instruction is to question platform claims and documentation rather than assume published guidance is what is actually executed.
Apply the same scepticism to platform guidance and claims more broadly: a Meta-suggested change, a documented metric, or a publicly stated best practice still needs to prove itself in your account.
caveats: The earnings-report link and the claim that Meta does not follow its own rules are the presenter's theory, not verified information, and he explicitly says he cannot go into specifics. This card is not a compliance strategy and should not be treated as advice on evading policy.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx

cards.title: Treat facebook internally reported numbers as untrusted until externally verified
cards.summary: The presenter argues that Facebook is a for-profit company that optimizes for the most revenue from the largest advertisers, so internal platform metrics and recommendations should not be treated as neutral guidance.
cards.use_when: Reviewing performance reports or vendor claims for a store's Meta spend, or deciding how much weight to give Meta's own optimization scores when making budgeting decisions.
steps: Separate the theory from reality in your decision-making: big accounts can profitably run on lowest-cost auto bidding or bid caps, so don't assume manual bidding is a universal upgrade.
Test before you trust a claim. The presenter's example: identical creative can be approved for one advertiser and rejected for another, so do not treat a documented best practice as binding.
Build your own measurement trail. If you rely on Facebook-reported CPA or EMQ scores, you are making decisions on a number the platform itself controls; use third-party attribution instead.
caveats: The earnings-report-to-ban-wave explanation is the presenter's theory and is not verified; treat 'Facebook doesn't play by the rules' as an opinion, not a fact. Public data on ban waves and earnings correlation is not established here.
cards.source_name: the entire meta ads algorithm explained in 21 mins.docx
